title: Smoother CLI UX for site key lifecycle (create/list/revoke)
description:
Hit while wiring Pilobol.us to use Auritus instead of ElevenLabs Audio Native (2026-09-14). Three rough edges in the same session:

1. 'auritus site create' output prints 'site_id=None' -- the API response
   has no 'id' field, only 'site_key'. But 'auritus site revoke <ARG>' takes
   a 'site_id' argument (per --help and commands/site.py::revoke), and the
   printed site_id is useless for that call. Worked out empirically that
   passing the site_key itself to 'site revoke' succeeds (revoke_site() just
   DELETEs /sites/{arg}), so site_key IS the real identifier server-side --
   but nothing in the CLI says so, and the site_id=None line is actively
   misleading. Either stop printing site_id, or rename the revoke argument/
   help text to site_key, or have create actually return a real id.

2. 'auritus site revoke --help' crashes outright:
   TypeError: TyperArgument.make_metavar() takes 1 positional argument but 2
   were given
   Full traceback bottoms out in typer/rich_utils.py rich_format_help ->
   click get_usage_pieces -- looks like a typer/click version mismatch in
   this env (miniconda3 site-packages) specific to Argument (vs Option)
   metavar formatting. Every other --help (site create, site list, player)
   worked fine; only the Argument-based revoke command's help path hits this.
   Pin/bump the typer+click pair, or avoid the code path (e.g. give
   site_id a default via Option instead of a bare Argument) so --help doesn't
   500 on every command.

3. 'auritus site list' prints unreadable rows for real, existing sites:
   'None\torigin=None\tkey=None' x2 -- format string in the list command
   isn't matching the actual response shape from the API (something like the
   id/origin/key field names it expects don't match what /sites GET actually
   returns). Should at minimum print the site_key so a developer can tell
   their sites apart without guessing.

None of these blocked the integration -- worked around all three by reading
commands/site.py and api.py source directly -- but a developer without repo
access would be stuck. Low urgency, real friction.
